blocks.x: All right, today is April 16th, 1969, and I'm interviewing Alan Jaffe. Okay, Alan, could you tell me the story about how Preservation Hall started? Larry, Larry Borson had sessions in the hall, and was in his art gallery, associated artists, and I think about five years, going back to about 19, I think it was 1955 or 7, somewhere around there, where he started having Punch come over and play. Kid Thomas was playing there, and the Bazooka Trio used to play in Power of Ryan, and Patio, and they used to come over and play in there, and gospel singers and things. They'd come by, I don't know, according to him, sometimes several times a month, sometimes several months without having any activity. This was in what is now Preservation Hall? Yes. I think they also had some sessions next door in the dress shop or something. What was that? That was, they didn't happen to let Preservation Hall began. Oh, okay. When Preservation Hall became a, you know, sort of a full-time activity over here, in the building's now Preservation Hall, Larry moved this gallery next door into the dress shop, and we used to put on non-union things over there, like Billy and Dee Dee used to play there every, Preservation Hall, and then Preservation Hall closed one night a week, and that night we used to run a concert next door for Billy and Dee Dee. Then they used to have Sunday morning gospel things over there. Remember that thing that George Lewis did with Alfred Williams, the gospel singer? Mm-hmm. That was done on a Sunday morning, the gospel. Anyway, um, Ken Mills, when he first came to town, when he did the, the punch, the first punch record, he talked to Larry about having a place where the bands could, you know, rehearse. At that time they used the patio more than, you know, they recorded back here. Now, that was 1960, I know that. Yeah. Do you remember the month? Did they make the record? I mean, they talked about the time when you weren't here. No, it wasn't Ken. You weren't here, Ken Harris. I can't believe. Where did you get to town? In your, uh, March of 61. Okay, so, anyway, okay, so I just wondered if you had that, that doesn't really matter. I think it's on the line of notes of, uh, I'm sure that was here. Uh, at that time, uh, Larry, you know, talked to Ken about doing, uh, about, you know, running the concerts, and he was interested primarily in doing a series of recordings. Uh, he was, he had, uh, 61, he had come to town, I don't know, when he got here after the time, I'm sure I remember. So, I, I wasn't that much earlier than, than we got here. I think we used to, uh, because when we first got here, I know when we met Larry, Gary's introduced us to Ken as having a, just come back. Uh, there was, at that time, Ken was here. Uh, let me just stop this room, okay. Uh, so, when we first got here, uh, the first, the first music we actually heard was, other than, you know, Paddock and famous store, was driving down St. Peter Street, we saw some guys from Eureka Brass Band, it was, uh, Sheik and Chicken Henry, and they'd stopped in the Bill Russell shop, and we parked and talked to them, they were playing at the buildup, and we went with them to that concert, and then, after the concert, went over to Larry's gallery, which then we went to, it was, you know, it's now the dress shop, not the preservation wall, because he had already, you know, moved his, his, his gallery. And, um, at that time, when we met Ken, I think, uh, Dick Allen, Dick Allen had talked at the, at the, the buildup, and Bill Russell. Well, we met Bill before, because the musicians had gone into Bill's shop. Um, this was very short, this was shortly after you arrived, you know. Yeah, a couple weeks. And, um, let's see, I don't remember if, if, if Dierup was here then. Who? Andy Dierup, you know, from Storyville Records, he was here working with Bill Russellman, on his wife. If they weren't here then, they, they came here very shortly. Yes? The baby turned over by himself. I believe you. What's his name? Russell. Oh, really? Yeah. Russell. Russell Orens. Russell what? Russell Orens. Right. Oh. Um. I don't, I'm trying to think of when the first session was in the hall that we went to. It was on a Sunday, and I keep thinking it was around Mother's Day, but it was before Mother's Day, because Mother's Day we went to a parade, you know, across the river to have a parade every year on Mother's Day out in the country. I'm pretty sure it was before that there was a session, and it was, the band used to play that in the back of the hall used to play over by the, by the back, the back door. Yeah. And it was, the band used to play that in the back of the hall, it used to play over by the, by the back, the back door. Yeah. And it was, the, it was, the two carinets, Israel Borman and George. There's a photograph of that session. Nelson and George Gaynor and I think Cielos came in for a while. Punch was playing. Were these sessions in the afternoon? Yeah. They were Sunday afternoon. And it was not so much like a session in the room, it was more like a party. Everybody used to, you know, bring in, you know, beer and everybody just sit around. The band, you know, the band in play as continuously as it does now. We play a number again. Everybody would talk, we would move around and stuff, and then, you know, five minutes or so later they'd decide to play another number. And, you know, there'd be a lot of discussion about everything. You know, we, we got talking then with, with people, you know, because, you know, we were so disappointed. We expected to, to find, you know, a lot more music here in town. We, I guess we had the, you know, the Folkway Series Four Records that had just come out shortly before we came down here, maybe down six months ago. I really thought that, you know, all these people, you know, were still playing and, you know, it was relatively easy to get to hear. We got talking to, oh, Mrs. Willis and people, you know, Larry, and she had suggested, you know, that these things, you know, be done. Ken was willing to take, you know, the responsibility of, of hiring the bands and, you know, things like that, but he didn't want to actually get involved and, you know, passing the kitty and sweeping the floors and stuff like that. Yeah. Um, so, you know, Larry always used to, we used to, didn't use a kitty, used to use one of the big bands to pick up the plates. And, uh, I say it was the first concert we came to, you know, we ended up handing Sandy the plate, and, you know, she, um, was, you know, he, you know, he always tended, he always wanted, you know, like, I know, uh, you know, Diane Lazor, I remember she worked for Larry and she used to, you know, work to collect, clean me. Um, so, Sandy, you know, more or less said that she would, you know, collect and that myself, you know, would try to, you know, we had, we still had a lot of trouble, you know, trunks coming in and stuff, you know, someone had to be there to, you know, put them out. So I used to, I used to help Larry or whoever else was there, and, uh, and, you know, we were an advocate, viewers and folks for the band and stuff. Um, well, when did the whole staff giving concerts in the evening on a more or a nightly basis? Um, we used, uh, a lot of people, uh, we used, we used June something as an anniversary, didn't I know? June 15th, I think, something like that. And that was the date that we started taking Union Scale. And the whole, as long as the band ran on, you know, you know, on an occasional basis, not on any, you know, any type of, you know, it was just, it was just Sunday afternoons, really. And then went to nightly concerts. And we ran for about, you know, two weeks, maybe, maybe three before, you know, before we had a, no. Nightly? Yeah. No, it was running nightly. I was saying, it ran nightly maybe two weeks before, you know, before June 15th. So, you know, it started right around June 1st, I guess. Well, some of the, I was going to say, it was around Mother's Day, which was the beginning of May, that, you know, everybody, you know, sort of got together and we started talking about it. Well, when were these, these, this, this started as far as, can you tell me about this? Yeah, okay. When the war was running, it was, you know, Larry sort of, you know, although, you know, like, he, no one, we weren't paying, no one was paying any rent. Um, and, uh, Larry, you know, sort of, you know, approved everything, you know, or disapproved of everything that went on. Um, like, like Barbara Reed wasn't involved in it, you know, at that time, because Larry, you know, sort of, you know, disapproved of her being involved in it. Larry went to get married. And he was away for about, what, two weeks? Maybe three weeks? He got married in San Francisco and then he drove cross-country and stuff. I'm sorry, you have any memories that you can go down. Who were the people in this, this so-called society would have installed and started to think of? Do you remember?
Do you think she really picked up my stupid thing? I don't know.
You have to say something. Say something. Can you remember the people who were there?

The people of the Society for the Preservation, the traditional chap, there's Barbara Reed, Mrs. Willis, Bill Russell, Mills, you know, Larry still must have the original, um, papers that were drawn on the form of the Society for the Union and the other square. Okay, now it's going. You were still talking?
No, I just asked her about the people who were in the Society and then, but... Who were members? Walter Eisling, you mentioned?
Oh, no, no. Walter, nice. You know who he is?
A photographer somehow, isn't he? Yes, but he was also a drama teacher at, um, being to the University in New York, he was Belgium. And, uh, uh, uh, Mrs. Willis, and... Sophie Shannon.
Oh, yes, Sophie. I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

The officers of the Society were... Ken, Barbara... Uh... Ken, Barbara, Sylvia, Mrs. Willis... And I was... What's her call? Sergeant at Arms. You were? Thank you, sir. Wow. Can you tell me? You said you, too.
I didn't want to do the Marines, though they used to be held fired. We had to be held privately. Yeah, we had to be...
I would, you know, like... The four, you know, board members were, uh, you know, like, Barbara and Ken and... But Sylvia didn't go to meetings, either.
She went to a couple of Larry's sentences.
No, she sent Mrs. Willis.
Sent Mrs. Willis, too.
Yeah.
But he sent Sylvia to make sure Mrs. Willis has three of his instructions properly. And he was...

Well, can you... Well, what we were saying before is you told him about when, you know, the whole thing... So the whole thing actually took place, you know, in a couple weeks that... In a couple weeks that, uh, you know, Larry was away. Well, not... The Society was founded, and, you know... Oh, he was on that one, he was away. Yeah, well, he went to get married. Yeah. And... It was in that time that... The Society only, you know, I don't think lasted a month. Did it? No. No. So I'm saying it must have been going for two weeks while Larry was away. And two weeks after he came back. Okay. And that was it. Well, can you tell me about this time that there was a sort of a transfer of power, you might say, in the hall when... Because originally, or initially, I believe Ken Mills was, as you say, sort of hiring a band. Yeah. And Larry went away. And Larry went away. Yeah. And also... Also making up the difference, you know, because... Yeah. At that time, band was just under a... Oh, of course, about 90... 93. 50, 92. 59. And, you know, we weren't... I would say that one of the weekend nights, you know, that they were making it, you know, that they were making it, you know, that they were making it, you know, and they were making it up to carry, you know, maybe cover up the deficit of two days, maybe, but they weren't, you know, it was not... Every week was running into a deficit. Yeah. Wow. So... Now, then he went... Larry went away, and there's some story about how... Anyway, you can tell him the story. Then Larry came back and said he got mad or something. Yeah. Well, he's, you know, he was mad. He was mad, first of all, because, you know, that, uh, you know, when he told him, this, I was, you know, the society says, you know, and, you know, he, like, you know, at first refused to, you know, you know, admit, you know, that there was, you know, such an organization. And, uh, everybody in the thing itself, you know, you know, sort of, sort of hassled. Uh, the minute there was an organization, you know, they wanted to schedule bands, you know, say, well, you know, I like this band, and, uh, people said, well, there was another group that said the leader should bring, you know, who he wants to bring, and another one said, you know, Ken felt, you know, that he wanted to, you know, pick the personnel. And, uh. Well, when, when did you take over the business of having bands, and generally running hall, as you do now, more or less? September. September of 61? Yeah. June, July, August. Yeah. The hall went for just about three months. Yeah. And it was running continuous, the whole life. Yeah. And it was running continuous. Yeah. How did you say that? It was running, were you running every night? It was running five, six nights a week, five nights a week a start. Well, we started off, you know, three nights a week, four nights a week a week, and, you know, I think we were running four nights a week when, you know, when the union said that it would give us a better rate if we went, you know, six nights a week. We went six nights a week. And sometimes one of the nightly concerts would be on a Sunday afternoon instead. It wasn't, you know, I mean, it was the hours of Chang, we used to run, oh, the one they finally settled on was eight to twelve. But there are other times that it ran, you know, earlier and later. We had schedules from those days. I know. I've got some of those fairly early schedules. I haven't got any of those fairly early ones, you know, whether they're not living out. We used to make them on a Jell-O, you know, on those Jell-O transfer plates. Remember? Yeah. Do you, um... That was when the Society was still going. To what extent have you been able to keep records, actually, over the years, of people who were playing at Preservation Hall? Well, we published a list one time. They were put in the back of a program or something. Some of the other schedules or something. Yeah. And... Um... So I don't know, you know, who was here necessarily on any given day, you know. A friend of mine came down here actually at that time and around about, I think it was around August of 61, and he, for many of you, of course, was very excited and he got back. All the bands for about two weeks. I know who else was here. A Japanese kid did the same thing. What's that? With a hearing aid. Oh, yeah. Uh, you know, Hero and a Mac. Yeah. Well, um, yeah, he was here. He was here from the very beginning. He must have been, you know, a member of the Society. How, uh, at the beginning of that you were charging, uh, just donations? Well, when it started, we had, we used to use the door behind the piano as the main entrance. Um, people came in there and we moved the band from the back of the room to the front of the room, pretty much once this concert started. There was a lot of argument about that, a lot of people. You know, these things were not just something that, you know, an argument about that would be a major meeting and, you know, everybody would... Uh, people, you wouldn't even ask people for money when they came in. No. You asked, you would, you would pass the kiddie.
You'd pass the kiddie just regularly, or regularly.

You know, you'd figure whenever, you know, there was enough new people at that, you know, a lot of bands playing, you know, would you, you'd usually get up a fast tune or something, and, you know, kind of go through it. And, you know, Sandy used to try to remember who she got, but she didn't, you know, people didn't put anything in, you know, to insult them, you know, put something in. But at that time, you know, someone put 25 cents in, you know, it was... I remember the first time I came in, I put a dollar in, you know, for the two of us at a gospel thing, you know, and, like, ooh, you know, like... And, you know, it was... But, but people would be approached, you know, to contribute, you know, twice a set, at least. Then we stopped, when we took over, we stopped passing the kiddie, and used to ask people to give money on their way out. And, and... And... No? Yeah.
So, I think that, even after, between September, and for the next few months, I would still pass on the kiddie, and so on. I think that was a little bit of a story. Yeah. I'm trying to...

See, we had a lot of trouble with the people across the street, noise problems. But we ended up closing the door behind the piano. Ione used to help us a lot, you know, and she used to stand over by the, by the gate. And no one came in the gate, you know. I don't mean no one, I mean, but, you know, in the course of the night, maybe, you know, five to ten people would actually, you know, come in that way. Most of the people come in that, the, the door is now closed. And... Uh, we closed that door, you know, like, you know, say, well, we, you know, keep the doors to the room closed. You know, we would stop complaining about the noise. And, uh, they did, as a matter of fact. You know, they complained about other things, but, I mean, they would stop complaining about the noise. And then we used to just use the... And when we went over there, that's when we just started asking people to put money in the kiddies they came in.
Yeah.
And we went, we moved the gate.
We moved the gate around the other side. We just used to say, you know, our bossy, and say, you know, do the hidden issue. And a lot of times people would be negative, actually.
Yeah. Then it went to fifty cents at some point, do you think?
But, no, we changed it because it was very hard to get inside to collect, because people would come in standing around the door.

Yeah. And so, you know, you would, a lot of people would get approached, you know, so many times, you know, and other people, you know, wouldn't, and, you know, it was sort of unfair. So, you know, it was always, you know, sort of, I felt bad, you know, walking in front of the band and asking for money. But anyway, and then, but at some point it went to fifty cents. And then a few, I don't know, a few years later it went to a dollar, which is this now. It went, you probably don't remember the dates. Yeah, I do remember when I went to a dollar.
So we went to a dollar? We went away.
What did we go for?

Everything that happened happened, you know, because it had to happen. Like, I couldn't get inside to collect people and come to, you know, stand at the inner carriage or at the door. I couldn't get inside at all. So I had to start asking people to make a donation. But, you know, we went away when somebody started asking for the keys that we made a donation, too. We went, was it Jack, was it Jack Beach? Yeah, he wouldn't like to go out on the city or something, he wouldn't like to go out on the city or something.
Oh yeah. I heard, you're the photographer. No, no, Jack.
Oh, John Beecher? No, B.J. and Jack. Yeah, Peers.

Peers, Jack Peers. Yes. Our next door neighbor, when we were living here, somebody from Philadelphia. He came over one night and said, this is no way to run a business. He took the thing. Well, first of all, he was six foot six, you know. I'd stand there, you know, just not let people in. We're out. I don't remember when we went to fifty cent minimum. But the dollar, I think it was the dollar, we went to, we left three ladies here watching the whole night. June Conn and two of her girlfriends, they're all lawyers. You probably know them. They're all, you know, they had that office, they had an office together. They were all getting it. And I don't know if we went out to play. We took a band, was the one we went to Boston.

Well, I knew when we looked, Dr. Orstin went back a bit. It was when they took us to Function Society, we went out with working with little angels. And we came home. And we walked into the door and one of the ladies wouldn't let me in because they were going to pay a dollar. And I was going to get down the two and grabbed my horn and said, hey, you know, please put a dollar in here if you want to come inside.

Well, can we touch the subject side to the actual musical aspects of the hall and the people that you were, how you decided to go about choosing a particular band and particularly is to be used in a book about George Lewis. What sort of role do you feel that George played in the development of the hall and it's, you know, kind of working out? He was one of the, you know, few musicians whose name I knew before I came here. You know, the people, you know, involved with the punk band, you know, records I heard, of the Eureka Brass Band, of actual musicians' names. And then after we got to town, you know, and we'd talk to people about, you know, where can I get to hear music and stuff, most of them would always, you know, they would also, you know, talk about George Lewis as one, you know, named musician. Maya Shermer, you know, the woman whose work was Wisconsin, you know, and she knew, you know, because he went to Europe and things. And, you know, he had, he had the reputation then, you know, the same as that, like, the look story reputation, as being the last, you know, pure musician in town. The musicians himself, I think, you know, sort of thought of him as, you know, just another, you know, guy hustling for a job. I mean, even, you know, at that time. He was playing, you know, the first time, you know, we went to a session in the hall. And I remember, you know, Dick Allen, you know, saying, you know, that's George Lewis, you know, when he came in, you know, he pointed out.
Tom Decker, his human and Russell, came over for the first time.

And, right when the hall started, George left town. And he never played at the hall, you know, when it was actually a hall. And he was, the first time he really started playing, he came back from a trip. Where'd he go in, 61? I think he went. To Europe? To the Dardy Tate. Yeah. Yeah. He came back. He came over, came over here, went back, and I asked him if he would like to bring in a band. And he said, no, he would rather, you know, be a sideman. So he started playing with Thomas' band. And, oh, he played with them maybe three or four times, and then they did the Humboldt Rinkley program. But, you know, well, you probably know the dates of that tour, you know, when he went to Europe. I'm pretty sure that he was out of town, you know, all during, you know, the actual, you know, real beginning of the hall. I think he went sometime in the early fall or something. I'm gonna learn about that, but I'm just not sure. He could have made two coffee trips at that time. But I think he went there between and done some kind of an autograph. Just a brief trip, went on another trip, I don't know. He went so many times, I've never even had a piece of people like this. You know about the time he went over to make the appearance on the Aquabolt show? Yeah. He flew over and flew right back. That may be the time I was sitting there. But for another repertoire. He also went back to books too. Yeah. That was just how the doctor takes books. Yeah. Yeah. Um, uh, but as I say, I'm pretty sure that, you know, that he, you know, I, I, I, I, I, I hadn't even thought about that before. But he was, I remembered him coming back, you know, and I specifically remember him saying, you know, he didn't want to be a leader of a band. Mm-hmm. And also, uh, you know, the other musicians didn't want to play with him. That's how Sales ended up, you know, being leader of that, you know, the George Lewis band. You know, Kit Howard, Jim. Oh, the, the second role star. Yeah. Was that a leader of that? Yeah. He was the only one who had to play with the band. And, uh, the only other person who was suitable, you know, to everybody else in the band was Joe. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I don't remember why we didn't use Joe as leader. Except that we probably thought it was better to take somebody who wasn't, you know, associated with it at all. So Sales became leader, but, you know, he sort of understood that, you know, he, he knew why he was, he was the leader of the band, you know. And, uh, you know, he was leader. But everybody came to pick up their dates, you know, separately, you know, like, he, he didn't call the guys in the band. You know, he just paid the tax and stuff like that. Of course, George was still playing with Jim in those days, wasn't he? On the regular basis. He played with them all the way through on the regular basis. Yeah. Because we used to have a quartet then, you know, four pieces. There was Joe and, I guess, Joe Robichaud played piano. Joe Robichaud, Joe Watt, and Jim and George. But the piano players had changed. Sometimes they used Charlie Hammond for a while, they used Dolly Adams for a while. There was never any, you know, one regular piano player with them. But they played together, you know, until we stopped using quartets.
Remembering quartets?
Yeah. I don't remember when we stopped using quartets today.
Yeah.
Yeah.
There's a lot of good music there.
Yeah, really did you like that?
Yeah, that's one of the best places of George's is for me.

How do you feel that, um, how do you feel about the gradual erosion of musicians, how do you feel about George, George's dying in the legend of the Hall? Do you feel it affects the Hall very much? It affects me, you know. I certainly, you mean financially? No, I don't, I miss hearing them, you know.
The same way maybe, you know, Caruso kept the, you know, the Metropolitan Alphurs.

Yeah, you know, it went on and got bigger, but I think it's, you know, like, I don't know, there's, you know, like maybe a dozen, you know, really, you know, key musicians. And, you know, people who are, you know, really worth, you know, listening to. And, you know, they can carry a band, they can make a band, you know, soundbite, you know, put Jim with a weak band, you know, and you can carry it, you know, like, Percy can take, you know, a weak band by himself, you know. And just, you know, the difference of what he's playing, you know, make, you know, the band interesting. You know, Thomas can, you know, George was, you know, one of those musicians. He also, you know, was, you know, someone who I, you know, particularly, you know, like listening to. And, you know. Can you remember, let me see if you can ask this, you remember that time in the summer of 63 when George and Jim and Howard went on, more or less the same band, almost, but went on a short floor. I remember I heard, I was meant to be up playing up in the mountain. Can anyone hear that? Yeah.
No, he went away. He had a plane ticket so he flew away.

I can still get the bus if I can get a cab. Okay. If I can get a cab, I'll miss the plane too, of course. I should have left you at 12 o'clock. It's not 12 o'clock yet. I know, but I'd have to leave here at 12. So look, so you better cancel it right now before, while it's still time. I wonder if I can call in here to get a cab? Uh-huh. Well, uh, let's say I already asked you, I guess, about George's role and so on in the graphic of Preservation War. Do you, just talking about Preservation War in general, do you, how, do you, what sort of a role do you see it as playing in, uh, New York Jazz? Do you see it as a particular light or anything that's been taken away or a particular philosophy about it? I think the main thing that, you know, we always wanted to do is represent the music. I think we felt if people had a chance to listen to the music, you know, on a musician's own terms, uh, that, you know, it would be, at least, you know, successful enough to support itself. Uh, I think that, you know, the actual, you know, setting of the hall, you know, was something that, it was probably the way someone from out of town pictures, you know, what a place in New Orleans should look like. Yes. Uh, are you, you're satisfied or are you satisfied with that? Well, that's the way we want it. Yeah, I mean, yeah. Uh, do you ever wish it was any bigger? No. Um, it's a good size because you could still have, you know, five or ten, you know, five or ten people in there and then you can have three people in the hall and, you know, it looks like an audience. I always felt the one, you know, the most difficult thing was for the band to, you know, play in an empty room. So, you know, there were very few nights when there weren't anybody in there, but, you know, even so, in those nights, you know, Sandy and I could go in and sit in the hall, you know, and it looked like, you know, the, you know, there was, can I say, you know, five people could, you know. Did you actually have nights a lot of anybody in there? All my home? No. But, but we had nights. We had nights. Oh, yes. It was very difficult, you know, like, to, you know, when you opened, if no one came in frequently, like, you know, for the first half hour. So, you know, you think maybe, you know, maybe this is going to be the night when nobody came. Why did the sort of change in the forties occur in the general, I mean, but it seems to me that there was some point when there was a change in the sense that people would walk by a preservation hall and they'd say, that's preservation hall, whereas before that they might just say, well, what's that place? Well, the biggest change actually came last year, two years ago. You know, it was the first time, you know, people who, you know, you know, I mean, large crowds of people, you know, actually, you know, came to preservation hall because, you know, looking for it. When we first opened, you know, people just wandered it. And then for the next couple of years, there were, you know, people who came here, you know, specifically, but it was, you know, just a small amount of people. segments.title: Origins of Preservation Hall and the Jaffes' arrival in 1961
segments.summary: Jaffe tells how Larry Borenstein's gallery hosted informal sessions, then how he and Sandy arrived in March 1961, met musicians and Ken Mills, and began helping at the Sunday afternoon sessions that became nightly concerts.

segments.title: Members and officers of the Society for the Preservation of traditional jazz
segments.summary: Jaffe and the interviewer try to recall who belonged to the short-lived Society and who held office.

segments.title: Larry away, the Society's dispute, and taking over the bands in September 1961
segments.summary: While Borenstein was away getting married the Society tried to run the hall and lost money; Jaffe then took over booking, moving to nightly, six-night union-rate concerts.

segments.title: Passing the kitty and closing the door over noise complaints
segments.summary: How donations were collected at the start, the neighbours' noise complaints, and moving the gate and door.

segments.title: Raising admission to fifty cents and a dollar
segments.summary: Recollections of the price going up, enforcing it at the door, and a story of a band returning to find they had to pay.

segments.title: George Lewis's reputation and role in the hall
segments.summary: Asked about George Lewis, Jaffe says he was one of the few names he knew before coming and was seen as the last pure musician in town.

segments.title: George Lewis away at the start, Sales as bandleader, and the quartets
segments.summary: George left town as the hall began, declined to lead, and played as sideman; Sales became leader of the band, and the quartet with Jim and others is recalled.

segments.title: Losing George Lewis and the key musicians who carry a band
segments.summary: Jaffe says George's death affects him personally and that a dozen key musicians like Percy and Jim can make a weak band interesting.

segments.chapter: Touring and the future of the hall
segments.title: Philosophy of the hall, audiences, the 1963 New England tour, Japan, and the future
segments.summary: A long answer on representing the music, the hall's size and crowds, the summer 1963 tour with George Lewis, the Japan tour, the aging musicians, touring, and college audiences.
